author: Donny Meacham
title: Riley Keough + John Travolta Paternity Lawsuit - NewsBreak
text:
By Donny Meacham ,
2 hours ago
Riley Keough’s name has been unexpectedly pulled into a peculiar legal complaint involving her family — and an eyebrow-raising, unverified claim about John Travolta and his late wife, Kelly Preston.
According to TMZ , Keough — the daughter of Lisa Marie Presley and Danny Keough — is alleged in court documents to have once donated eggs that were later used by Travolta and Preston to conceive their now 15-year-old son, Benjamin.
Where the Claim Comes From The claim does not originate from Keough or Travolta. Instead, it appears in an amended lawsuit filed by two of Priscilla Presley ’s former business associates — Brigitte Kruse and Kevin Fialko — against Priscilla’s son, Navarone Garcia.
In that filing, the plaintiffs allege that following Lisa Marie’s death in January 2023, her ex-husband Michael Lockwood made a series of claims about internal family matters.
Read More: Priscilla Presley Reveals She Instructed Lisa Marie to Hide That She Was Elvis’ Daughter: WATCH
Among them was the assertion that Travolta and Preston had once considered using Lisa Marie’s eggs — and that Keough ultimately donated hers instead.
What the Filing Alleges The documents further claim that Keough was given a modest payment and an older Jaguar vehicle in exchange for the donation.
However, the filing does not provide any proof to support the claim, and none of the individuals named — including Keough, Travolta, or their legal representatives — have commented publicly or confirmed any such arrangement.
According to E! News , Priscilla slammed the paternity claim, calling it “shameful,” and it will be “addressed in court.”
The Bigger Picture The claim is part of a broader legal dispute centered on alleged financial and estate-related tensions within the Presley family.
Read More: Priscilla Presley Accused of ‘Pushing’ Elvis to His Death With Financial Pressure [REPORT]
According to the lawsuit, the information was brought up as part of negotiations aimed at securing a settlement for Lockwood and his daughters.
Travolta, 71, and Preston, who passed away in 2020, had three children together: Jett (who died in 2009), Ella Bleu, and Benjamin, born in 2010.
35 Country Music Lawsuits That Left Fans Shocked The music business is a high-stakes, high-risk venture, and it's not unusual for artists to wind up in court to defend their interests, as we'll see in this gallery of the nastiest country music lawsuits. Gallery Credit: Sterling Whitaker Brett Carlsen/Rick Diamond/Kevin Winter, Getty Images Ian Gavan, Getty Images Dolly Parton vs. Porter Wagoner Dolly Parton got her first big national break when Porter Wagoner cast her on his variety show, but the two had a falling out when she left to pursue a solo career in 1972. In 1980 he sued her for $3 million in damages. The pair settled out of court, and reconciled by the end of Wagoner's life in 2007. She was at his bedside when he passed away. Brett Carlsen, Getty Images Morgan Wallen vs. Disgruntled Fan Morgan Wallen faced a lawsuit from an angry fan after he canceled a concert in Oxford, Miss., at the last minute in April of 2023. Brandi Burcham filed a lawsuit against the singer, alleging that he had cost her significant damages in concert ticket fees that had not been refunded, as well as out-of-pocket expenses for travel, lodging, food and more. She asked a judge to make it into a class action suit. She later dropped the suit, but vowed to file another. Christopher Polk, Getty Images Carrie Underwood vs. Ron McNeill and Georgia Lyons Songwriters Ron McNeill and Georgia Lyons sued Carrie Underwood and her "Something in the Water" co-writers, Brett James and Chris DeStefano, claiming they stole from their song of the same title. Underwood says neither she nor her co-writers ever heard the other song. A statement from a rep said her song is a "deeply personal song regarding Carrie’s faith and she is saddened that anyone would attempt to challenge that for financial gain." Christopher Polk, Getty Images Jimmie Allen vs. Jane Does A woman identifying herself as Jane Doe sued Jimmie Allen in May of 2023, accusing him of rape, sexual assault and harassment that she says took place while she worked for him. Another woman sued in June with more sexual assault allegations.
Allen has since countersued both women, and settled with one. Kevin Winter, Getty Images Luke Combs' Legal Team vs. Nicol Harness Luke Combs' legal team filed suit against a fan named Nicol Harness in 2023, accusing her of selling unauthorized merchandise because she had sold a handful of Combs-themed tumblers on Amazon for $20 each to raise money for her medical bills. A judge ordered her to pay $250,000, but Combs intervened, saying he did not authorize or even know about the lawsuit. Combs began working on freeing her from the judgment, and he also sent her enough money to double her existing profits, as well as setting up an official tumbler online, with the profits slated to go toward her bills. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Tim McGraw vs. Curb Records Tim McGraw came out on top after Curb sued him for breach of contract in 2011. He counter-sued to get out of his contract, which he claimed was unfair and onerous. In 2013, after years of filings and hearings, McGraw triumphed when a judge threw out the last of Curb's claims, and he was able to record for Big Machine. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Travis Tritt vs. Category 5 Travis Tritt went to court against Category 5 Records when the label closed just after releasing his 2007 album, The Storm . Six years of litigation followed, and Tritt ultimately regained control of the masters for that album, releasing them in a modified form in 2013 via his own record label as The Calm After... . Frederick Breedon, Getty Images Clint Black vs. Bill Ham Clint Black ended up in court with the manager who had helped him launch his career. In 1992, Black sued Bill Ham over disagreements arising from management agreements and publishing rights, claiming Ham had breached his contract. The litigation dragged on for seven months before reaching an undisclosed settlement. Black later sued another manager/financial adviser, Charles Sussman, in 2008. Charley, Gallay, Getty Images Kenny Rogers vs. Capitol Records You don't want to mess with the Gambler. Kenny Rogers filed suit against Capitol Records in 2012, seeking $400,000 that he claimed he hadn't been paid due to accounting errors, as well as unspecified damages from what he said were unpaid digital royalties the label had deliberately under-reported. It's unclear if the case has ever gone to court. Frazer Harrison, Getty Images Brad Paisley vs. Sony Brad Paisley filed suit against his label, Sony, in 2010, claiming that he was owed at least $10 million in unpaid royalties. He filed an amended complaint in 2014 focusing on digital royalties, prompting Sony to ask a judge to throw the case out. The case has yet to be heard in court. Erika Goldring, Getty Images Garth Brooks vs. Lisa Sanderson Garth Brooks filed suit against a former friend and business partner, Lisa Sanderson. She was the CEO of his TV production company, and she sued Brooks after it closed, claiming he owed her back pay and retirement. He counter-sued, and a jury ultimately rejected her claims and awarded Brooks $226,000, which included loans he gave her, costs and attorney fees. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Naomi Judd Estate vs. Michael P. Dolan Naomi Judd's former manager, Michael P. Dolan, filed a lawsuit against the late singer's estate in April of 2023. He claimed he was still owed money from a 2000 television special he had been involved in, and that Judd had never settled with him prior to her death. He asked the court to order a full accounting of the money owed to him. It's not clear if the suit ever made it to court. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Brad Paisley and Carrie Underwood vs. Lizza Connor Singer-songwriter Amy Bowen, known professionally as Lizza Connor, sued Paisley, Underwood and the songwriters behind their hit "Remind Me" for $10 million, claiming the song was stolen from a song of hers by the same name. In 2016 a judge ruled against her in court. Scott Gries, Getty Images Sugarland vs. Kristen Hall Sugarland originally consisted of three members when the group burst onto the scene in 2005, but by the following year, Kristen Hall had departed for unspecified reasons. In 2008 she filed a $1.5 million lawsuit against her former bandmates, claiming that she had been unfairly deprived of money owed to her. That lawsuit was settled in 2010, and the terms have never been disclosed publicly. Ethan Miller, Getty Images LeAnn Rimes vs. Wilbur Rimes and Curb In May of 2000, LeAnn Rimes filed suit against her father, Wilbur Rimes, and another former manager, accusing them of misappropriating as much as $8 million over five years. That November she sued Curb Records to get out of what she claimed was an unfair deal her parents had signed on her behalf. She later settled and reconciled with her father, while a judge threw out her suit against Curb. Christopher Polk, Getty Images Heidi Merrill vs. Carrie Underwood, the NFL + More A struggling songwriter named Heidi Merrill filed suit against Carrie Underwood, the NFL, Underwood's producer Mark Bright and more in June of 2019, claiming Underwood's Sunday Night Football theme song, "Game On," was lifted from a song by the same title that Merrill submitted to Bright previously. Kevork Djansezian, Getty Images Taylor Swift vs. David Mueller Taylor Swift and former Denver radio personalty David Mueller were involved in a series of court dates after he sued her, claiming she got him fired. She countersued, accusing him of groping her at a meet and greet in 2013. Judges threw out all of Mueller's claims, and in August of 2017 a jury sided with Swift in her groping case against Mueller. Theo Wargo, Getty Images Kid Rock vs. Feld Entertainment Kid Rock renamed his Greatest Show on Earth Tour due to a lawsuit from Feld Entertainment, which owns Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus. The group has a trademark on the phrase. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Tim McGraw and Faith Hill vs. Sean Carey and Beau Golden Songwriters Sean Carey and Beau Golden filed suit against Tim McGraw, Faith Hill, Ed Sheeran and more, claiming the couple's song "The Rest of Our Life" was taken from a song they wrote titled "When I Found You." The suit has not gone to court yet. Michael Loccisano, Getty Images John Rich vs. Jared Ashley John Rich landed at the center of an enormous legal battle in 2009, when he sued former Nashville Star contestant Jared Ashley for defamation after Ashley accused him of punching him in the face. Ashley counter-sued, and Rich ultimately filed suit against Chris Sevier, the owner of Ashley's label, who had previously tangled with the singer over copyrights. Bizarrely, Rich later had Sevier arrested after he accused him of stalking the singer. Monica Schipper/Amy Sussman, Getty Images Taylor Sheridan vs. Cole Hauser Yellowstone creator Taylor Sheridan and series star Cole Hauser (Rip Wheeler) ended up at odds over coffee, of all things. Hauser launched his own brand of coffee called Free Rein in 2023, and it wasn't long before Sheridan's Bosque Ranch filed suit against the actor's new business, claiming trademark infringement and unfair competition. The issue is the logo, which bears a strong resemblance to the Bosque Ranch logo and caused concerns that fans would mistake the brand for Sheridan's own line of coffee. It's unclear if the suit will progress to a court hearing, or the warring parties might have settled out of court. Terry Wyatt, Getty Images Tyler Pride vs. Charley Pride's Estate Tyler Pride filed a lawsuit in May of 2021, seeking to dispute late singer Charley Pride's will. He alleged Pride was his father after an affair with his mother and sought recognition and compensation from his estate. Pride had a DNA test to back up his assertions, and in 2022, he revealed he had reached a settlement with the estate, though the terms are undisclosed. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Martina + John McBride vs. Richard Hanson A former employee named Richard Hanson sued Martina McBride and her husband, John McBride, in June of 2018, alleging they had mistreated unpaid interns who worked at their recording studio, Blackbird, over the years, then fired him when he filed an official complaint with the state. In February of 2020, a jury awarded him $100,000 in compensatory damages, $59,000 in back pay and $59,000 in liquidated damages after finding that the McBrides fired him in retaliation. Isaac Brekken, Getty Images Katie Armiger vs. Cold River Records Katie Armiger and her former label, Cold River Records, have traded lawsuits since 2016, when the label sued her for alleged breach of contract. She fired back with a lawsuit that shook Nashville's establishment with allegations of sexual harassment, saying her label encouraged her to flirt with, kiss and sit in the laps of radio programmers to try to garner airplay. After they reached a private settlement, Cold River sued Armiger again in 2017 after she gave an interview to Fox News about the #MeToo movement. She has since filed a complex countersuit alleging a wide list of alleged improprieties against her former label.
Armiger later settled with Cold River. The terms of the settlement were undisclosed. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Angie Gentry vs. Helicopter Manufacturers After Montgomery Gentry singer Troy gentry died in a helicopter crash in September of 2017, his widow, Angie, filed a lawsuit in February of 2018 against Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation, Sikorsky Global Helicopters, Inc. and the Keystone Helicopter Corporation for wrongful death. The suit claims they failed to make the Model 269 helicopter that crashed and killed her husband crashworthy. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Customers vs. Dollywood Dolly Parton's theme park, Dollywood, has faced two lawsuits in recent years from riders who claim they were injured on rides. In 2014, a woman claimed she suffered a permanent brain injury after falling from a ride called the Waltzing Swinger. In 2018, another woman and her husband sued for more than $2 million, alleging she had suffered spinal cord injuries after falling from a ride called the RiverRush Water Coaster. Rick Diamond, Getty Images Steve Earle + More vs. Universal Music Group Steve Earle is one of the artists leading a class action lawsuit against Universal Music Group over a fire that destroyed more than 800 artists' master tapes in 2008. A lawsuit filed in June of 2019 alleges UMG mishandled their tapes, then deliberately covered up the fire and excluded the affected artists from the proceeds from insurance settlements and damage claims. Jason Kempin, Getty Images Josh Turner's Crew vs. His Bus Company and Management Several members of Josh Turner's crew filed suit against All Access Coach Leasing, bus driver Bradley Dratnol and Turner’s management company, Modern Management, in 2020 after a 2019 bus accident took the life of one crew member and left others with severe injuries.
The suit alleged wrongful death, negligent and defective design of the bus and wrongful hiring.
It's not clear from public reports if the case has ever gone to court. Jason Kempin, Getty Images Jellyroll vs. Jelly Roll Country singer and rapper Jelly Roll found himself on the receiving end of a lawsuit in 2024, when a dance band out of Pennsylvania called Jellyroll filed suit against him. The band said it had used that name since March of 1980, more than four years before the singer was born, and that his choice to use the same name had negatively impacted their branding.
They sued for service mark infringement, false designation of origin and/or sponsorship, dilution, common law palming off, trademark and trade name infringement and unfair competition, and injury to business reputation.
The band dropped the suit shortly afterward, revealing they had reached an "amicable agreement" with the singer. The terms remain undisclosed. Samuel De Roman, Getty Images Devyn LaBella vs. Kevin Costner A stuntwoman named Devyn LaBella filed suit against Kevin Costner and several production companies involved in his Horizon movie series in May of 2025, alleging she had been forced to film an "unscripted rape" scene as part of her work on the film, and without an intimacy coordinator on the set.
Her suit alleges sexual discrimination, harassment and creating a hostile work environment. She's seeking "general and compensatory damages in amounts to be proven at trial." The suit has yet to go to trial. Mike Windle, Getty Images Alexander Cardinale and Morgan Reid vs. Jake Owen Songwriters Alexander Cardinale and Morgan Reid filed suit against Jake Owen in 2021, alleging that his No. 1 hit, "Made for You," borrowed extensively from their song of the same title, which appeared in a national ad campaign in 2016.
It's not clear if the suit ever went to trial. Theo Wargo, Getty Images Jane Doe vs. Garth Brooks In October of 2024, a makeup artist and hairstylist filed suit against Garth Brooks, alleging that the country superstar had sexually assaulted her multiple times in 2019, while she was in his employ.
She also accused him of a pattern of verbal and physical abuse, which the singer has denied. He has also sued her, and a judge denied his request to have her lawsuit thrown out, but so far, the case has yet to go to court. Noam Galai, Getty Images Dawn Olivieri vs. Various Parties Yellowstone star Dawn Olivieri filed suit against multiple parties in July of 2024, alleging that they had been making false allegations that she had abused horses at Moon Mountain, a non-profit that she founded to rescue animals.
The lawsuit also alleged cyberstalking, trespassing at Moon Mountain and even making terroristic threats, which she says stems from one of the defendants saying she could be "unalived."
The result of that lawsuit is not clear. Jason Kempin, Getty Images Kellie Pickler vs. Her Former In-Laws Kellie Pickler's husband, famed Nashville songwriter Kyle Jacobs, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound in February of 2023 at the age of 49. Pickler filed suit against his parents, Sharon and Reed Jacobs, in November of 2024, alleging they had entered her home and removed items without her consent.
They have gone around and around in court ever since, with them alleging that Pickler is withholding items from them that are part of their son's estate, while she claims she either does not know where certain items are or no longer has them.
The lawsuit is currently ongoing.
